Title: An HPC Framework for Multi-Modal Plant Phenotyping Integrating Controlled Environment and Open Field Studies

Abstract
This paper presents a systemic framework designed to advance
multi-modal plant phenotyping research through the strategic use
of high-performance computing (HPC) in agricultural science. Our
framework addresses the unique challenges in high-throughput
plant phenotyping (HTP) research, which integrate multi-mode
imaging sensors such as RGB, hyperspectral, LiDAR, thermal, and
X-ray computed tomography (CT) across indoor and outdoor envi-
ronments. Our primary objective is to transform raw sensor data
into research-ready plant phenotypical traits. This directly sup-
ports downstream agricultural research, such as in plant breeding,
crop management, etc. The framework is structured into two main
phases. The initial data processing occurs on non-HPC systems,
utilizing operating system and license-specific software due to the
specialized algorithms and knowledge required for each imaging
data pipeline. The subsequent HPC phase refines these processed
datasets into tabular formats, preparing them for statistical analysis
in agronomy, plant science, and bioinformatics. The current im-
plementation of the second phase utilizes a hybrid parallelization
model across HPC nodes and threads. However, its performance
could be significantly enhanced by implementing more efficient
algorithms and optimizing resource allocation. We discuss current
bottlenecks, including technical challenges related to sensors, imag-
ing platforms, and computational pipelines, and propose immediate
solutions.

Introduction
Plant phenotyping quantitatively assesses plant traits influenced
by genetics and environment [1]. This field is a cornerstone of
modern agricultural and plant science, unraveling the complex in-
terplay between a plant’s genome, its environment, and key aspects
like growth, yield, and stress response. Conventionally, measuring
plant phenotypes involved laborious manual methods requiring sig-
nificant time and efforts. Advanced sensing technologies, coupled
with data-driven trait extraction and automation, have revolution-
ized this process, enabling more efficient and comprehensive data
collection [2].
Despite these advancements, significant bottlenecks persist
within plant phenotyping workflows. Researchers frequently en-
counter long waiting times for imaging and image data processing
requests, a lack of standardized processing steps, inconsistent data
formats, and unclear methods for leveraging generated data in
downstream analyses.
In this research, we introduce a holistic approach to streamline
high-throughput plant phenotyping using imaging systems in in-
door, controlled-environments or unmanned aerial vehicle-based
(UAV-based) imaging systems with high-performance computing
(HPC). Our primary objective is to generate a consolidated, tabular
measurement output. While this process entails some raw data
information loss, the resulting tabular format is highly practical
for agricultural researchers leveraging various statistical and data
science techniques.
Our paper outlines image data processing methodologies based
on imaging sensor modalities, differentiating between pre-HPC
processing and HPC utilization. This paper presents a novel ap-
proach to sensor-based HTP by implementing parallelization at
both the HPC node level and the thread level to enhance process-
ing performance. We also identify current bottlenecks and future
challenges within these pipelines. Finally, we present the observed

2
scope of work
The data framework in this study handles input from diverse indoor
and outdoor remote sensing sensors, all aimed at high-throughput
phenotyping (HTP) research. The primary challenge in HTP re-
search is converting large-size, multi-dimensional and often times
ambiguously formatted sensor datasets into a structure that agricul-
tural researchers can readily use. Raw imaging sensor data presents
a significant processing challenge due to its diverse and unstan-
dardized formats, which include varied geometric representations
and inconsistent data dimensions, alongside intrinsic data quality
issues. Our goal is to transform the raw sensor data into a tabular
matrix of plant traits that provides quantifiable measurements for
each experimental unit. This standardized format will empower
researchers to perform essential statistical analyses, obtain key
agronomic and plant science metrics, correlate measurements with
plant physiological parameters, and conduct advanced bioinformat-
ics analyses that integrate genetic information. This paper will not
extensively detail raw data quality control methodologies, given
their complexity and rapid technological advancements. However,
we will briefly address current challenges frequently encountered
by researchers.
A critical, yet often overlooked, aspect of successful high-
throughput phenotyping is accurately identifying the data of target
experimental unit within the large and complex sensor datasets.
Indoor experiments typically involve repeated scans or imaging of
specific plants. This necessitates deliberate labeling of each scan
with the target plant identifier (ID) and the timing of measurement.
This can be achieved by embedding information directly into the
scanned file or metadata using barcodes or quick response (QR)
codes. Outdoor experiments usually involve data collection via
sensors mounted on UAVs, observation towers, or spidercams [3].
For open-field experiments, experimental subjects (plots) remain
in fixed locations throughout the growing season, enabling their
geographical assignment and labeling by location. This necessi-
tates a field map detailing the spatial arrangement of plots and the
experiment design as defined by the researcher.
For robust statistical analysis, it is essential to accurately record
the experimental design and the environmental conditions associ-
ated with each experimental unit. Agricultural researchers com-
monly achieve this by documenting key details such as plant variety,
specific treatment applications, and relevant environmental param-
eters, e.g., weather and soil conditions.
3
SENSOR DATA FRAMEWORK
3.1
Data workflow prior to HPC integration
This section outlines the typical experimental process and data flow
in HTP research prior to HPC integration (Fig. 1). Initially, data
users define the experiment design and reserve space in either a
growth chamber, greenhouse or open field. Researchers and facility
managers then prepare and plant seeds, cultivating them under spe-
cific environmental conditions and management practices. During
the experiment, imaging data is collected on designated dates, typi-
cally determined by days after planting or specific growth stages.
Figure 1: Imaging data workflow prior to HPC integration.
The collected data then undergo initial processing on personal
computers (PCs) if the imaging pipeline requires licensed software
or a specific machine. This paper exemplifies the use of various
imaging pipelines within the Purdue Ag Alumni Seed Phenotyping
Facility (AAPF). While minor differences in system implementation
and software may exist across other facilities, the core principles
presented here are broadly applicable.
3.1.1
Indoor RGB Imaging Data. Each scan captures a single top
image and twelve side-view images, spaced 30° apart, covering
a full 360°. To differentiate vegetation from non-vegetation, raw
images are segmented using a registered, co-axil fluorescence im-
age collected concurrently with the RGB image. If a concurrent
fluorescence image is unavailable, RGB-based vegetation indices
can be used for the same segmentation purpose [4]. From the seg-
mented images, geometric traits (e.g., width, height, roundness,
area, center of mass, convex hull area) and colorimetric traits (e.g.,
hue, saturation, intensity statistics) are extracted and exported to
the parallel file system (PFS). Imaging systems, particularly for
plant phenotyping research like our indoor RGB imaging, often
include integrated software solutions that automate imaging, mech-
anize plant movement, optimize camera settings, and streamline
data curation. While extraction of above image-based traits can
be performed efficiently on consumer-grade PCs due to its low

computational demand, leveraging HPC can provide significant ad-

3.1.2
Indoor Hyperspectral Imaging Data (HSI).. Each scan cap-
tures top and side views using cameras that cover visible and near-
infrared (VNIR, 350-1000 nm), and shortwave infrared (SWIR, 1000-
2500 nm) region. The VNIR and SWIR cameras acquire data with
approximately 500 and 300 narrow wavelength channels within
their respective ranges. Due to the substantial input and output de-
mands of HSI data, the PCs connected to the HSI system primarily
serve to relay data from the cameras to the central storage.
3.1.3
Indoor X-ray Computed Tomography Data. Our research uti-
lizes an X-ray computed tomography (CT) imager to acquire com-
prehensive data on underground root architectures. The imaging
process involves rotating a plant pot within a shielded control
booth, allowing for the capture of attenuated X-rays from vari-
ous angles. Subsequently, the angular projection data undergoes
reconstruction to yield detailed root surface geometry. This recon-
struction primarily focuses on precise pixel-level segregation of
root and non-root components, and the geometric algorithm to
detect roots across a range of diameters [5]. The output of this pro-
cess is a comprehensive 3D root surface geometry represented by
points, edges, and facets. We use RootForce (Fraunhofer, München,
Germany), a vendor-licensed software, which is inherently tied
to specific personal computers that meet particular computing re-
source specifications. Challenges in accurately processing X-ray
CT data for root analysis include selecting optimal input parame-
ters for root delineation and defining the target region of interest
for varying container sizes. Due to substantial data volumes and
computational demands, data processing and quality assurance are
time-consuming, leading to delayed turnaround when results are
suboptimal. Currently, no open-source alternatives offer both the
necessary usability of the software and seamless integration with
the X-ray imaging systems.
3.1.4
UAV-based RGB Imaging Data. UAV RGB imagery is pro-
cessed using structure from motion and multi-view stereo (SFM-
MVS) to create a 3D model of the study area [6]. This model is
then orthorectified to produce a nadir-looking orthomosaic image.
While commercial software is often favored for its quality and ease
of use, open-source alternatives are also available such as Open-
DroneMap [7]. The accuracy of the orthomosaic largely depends
on the precision of the navigation data (sensor location and orien-
tation) and the distinctness of feature points within the raw images.
Utilizing high-precision global positioning system (GPS), such as
real-time kinematics (RTK) or post-processed kinematics (PPK), can
substantially improve accuracy. Ideally, drone flights should occur
in low wind conditions to ensure that the distribution of feature
points in consecutive images remains consistent.
3.1.5
UAV-based Hyperspectral Imaging Data (HSI).. Hyperspec-
tral data requires several crucial corrections after data collection.
Geometric distortions are rectified using available UAV navigation
and ground geometry data. Subsequently, radiometric calibration
transforms raw digital numbers into radiance or reflectance values.
Developing an independent processing chain for these steps can
be demanding, especially for users lacking extensive experience
with aerial hyperspectral data. Therefore, it is often advisable to
utilize data processing solutions offered by sensor or UAV platform
vendors. However, these vendor-provided solutions are typically
subject to licensing or machine constraints. A significant bottle-
neck in hyperspectral data processing stems from the inherent
complexity of geometric correction and the large data size.
3.1.6
UAV-based Light-Detection and Ranging Data (LiDAR).. Aerial
LiDAR data undergoes a precise post-processing step to refine the
position and orientation of the UAV. The UAV trajectory data is
then combined with the raw LiDAR ranging measurements to cre-
ate a georeferenced 3D point cloud with X, Y, and Z coordinates.
Optionally, this point cloud can also include LiDAR reflectivity of
the surface or RGB values obtained from concurrent flights. Vari-
ous point cloud refinement and quality control procedures can be
applied as needed, such as strip alignment, outlier filtering, and
smoothing. Due to the technical complexity of aerial LiDAR pro-
cessing, phenotyping service providers and researchers often rely
on data processing solutions provided by sensor or UAV platform
vendors. A key aspect of aerial LiDAR processing is the accurate
alignment between sensor and reference coordinate systems, as
well as managing large input and output data volumes.
3.1.7
UAV-based Thermal Imaging Data. Accurate thermal image
processing requires calibrating with ground target temperature
measurements. Our team employs multiple ground targets with
concurrent temperature measurement during flights to facilitate
a linear conversion of the raw thermal imaging data. Following
this calibration, a 3D model is generated using SFM-MVS, simi-
lar to the approach used for RGB images. A significant technical
challenge in thermal processing stems from the lack of distinctive
feature points in thermal images, particularly in crop fields where
surface temperatures can be uniform when vegetation completely
covers the ground. Establishing alleys between research plots can
greatly mitigate this issue. This challenge is compounded by the
intrinsically lower spatial resolution of thermal images, which is
due to the greater energy difference required in the 3-4 휇m thermal
wavelengths to register temperature variations. Consequently, even
with precise UAV navigation data, the geometric accuracy of the
resulting orthomosaic image can be suboptimal, often requiring an
additional georeferencing step. This step typically involves georef-
erencing with GPS surveyed points or image-to-image matching to
a preciesely-georeferenced RGB image employing unique ground
features.
3.2
Data workflow with HPC
Our team employs an HPC cluster for all subsequent data processing.
We currently offer three distinct imaging data pipelines for indoor
applications and four for UAV data (Fig. 2). We are meticulously
combining these disparate research pipelines into a single, more
cohesive and easily maintainable system.
3.2.1
Indoor RGB Imaging Data. The RGB-derived plant pheno-
types, obtained from each scan, serve as the input data and are
delivered in tabular format. We consolidate these dates from mul-
tiple dates and plants into two tabular files for side- and top-view
scans. This is a computationally inexpensive and fast step.

3.2.2
Indoor Hyperspectral Imaging Data (HSI).. The HSI data pro-
cessing pipeline involves three main steps, designed to maximize
data utility and address common challenges associated with HSI
cameras. First, the initial step involves checking the entire dataset
for the presence of all necessary files, including imaging data and
metadata. A detailed processing strategy is then generated for each
concurrent scan session. This is crucial because HSI cameras are
more prone to technical malfunctions than other imaging sensors in
our system. For example, if all data (VNIR and SWIR) are available
for at a specific time point and plant, the strategy will combine
VNIR and SWIR imaging data. However, if SWIR data are missing,
the strategy will adapt to use only VNIR data. A separate SLURM
job is submitted for each scan session to enable parallelization in
HPC (Fig. 3). Second, each smaller data processing job correspond-
ing to a specific time point and plant is executed. Within each job,
we perform radiometric calibration and co-registration of VNIR and
SWIR data [8]. Raw digital numbers are converted to reflectance
in the 0-1 range, achieved by applying dark current and white ref-
erence measurements from materials that virtually establish 100%
reflectivity. The VNIR and SWIR co-registration involves coarse
Affine transformation for approximate alignment, followed by a
precise registration step using an optimized transformation ma-
trix based on the enhanced correlation coefficient (ECC) criterion
[9]. Due to the large data size, both registration and warping are
computationally intensive. Reflectance spectra across the available
wavelength range and various vegetation indices are then calcu-
lated and exported in a tabular format. A hyperspectral datacube is
processed in parallel, with each core handling a separate instruction.
The number of parallel processes in a CPU is equal to the number of
Figure 3: Data parallelization scheme for indoor hyperspec-
tral imaging (HSI).
vegetation indices or wavelengths being analyzed (Fig. 3). Concur-
rently, supplementary data are generated to assess the VNIR and
SWIR co-registration quality, along with the resultant vegetation
indices. Third, we merge and organize the processed data. The
individual tabular datasets containing reflectance spectra and veg-
etation indices from each smaller data processing job are merged
into a unified dataset. Additionally, vegetation index images are
merged by their respective types (e.g., normalized difference vege-
tation index, enhanced vegetation index) [10]. This consolidation
significantly streamlines file transfer and management by reducing
number of files.
3.2.3
Indoor X-ray Computed Tomography Data. Excessive local
soil moisture in containers can create imaging artifacts in X-ray CT
root scans. While drying the pots helps, completely eliminating
these false root detections is not possible as excessive drying is
detrimental to the plant. Therefore, we remove disconnected false
roots and correct minor geometric errors in the vendor-generated
root surface to ensure seamless algorithm processing. Subsequently,
the refined root surface geometry data transforms into a skeleton,
which is a graph of nodes and edges, using a TEASAR-based method
[11, 12]. A necessary cleaning step is executed to address incon-
sistent details that may be present in the skeleton. From the root
surface geometry voxel, and skeleton models, we calculate and save
the total root length, root volume, root surface area, and average
root diameter for each scan. A comprehensive set of root traits is
obtained from the horizontal plane utilizing small increments along
the z-axis. First, the root crown (root collar) location is defined from
the scan. Then, a hypothetical horizontal plane is generated using,
e.g., 25 mm depth increments from the surface. The depthwise
root traits include the number of roots penetrating the horizontal
plane, the average root diameter at the specific depth, the average
horizontal distance from the root center (as projected to the current
plane) to individual roots, and the variation of the distances. As
a quality control measure, visualizations of the voxel model and

3.2.4
UAV-based RGB, HSI, Thermal Imaging Data. Input ortho-
mosaic images are used to derive plot-based traits. The image-
derived plant traits encompass the average spectral channel value
(reflectance spectrum for HSI data), temperature, plant canopy cov-
erage per unit area on the ground, and various vegetation indices
computed from spectral channels. Researchers must supply the
plot dimensions or experimental design to define the spatial bound-
aries of each plot within the dataset. This processing stage involves
importing large input image files to memory, yet each experimen-
tal plot is relatively small. Therefore, the primary computational
bottleneck lies in loading the images, conversely, extracting traits
for individual plots requires minimal computation. Calculating
vegetation indices also demands significant resources, with the
computational load directly proportional to the number of vegeta-
tion index types and the total number of plots. To leverage HPC for
parallelization, a separate SLURM job is submitted for each scan,
which typically represents data collected on a single date (Fig. 4).
The number of parallel processes in each node is configured to
match the number of plots being analyzed, allowing each thread to
independently handle a single plot.
4
RESULTS
The HPC-based data processing workflow was executed on the
Purdue Negishi HPC cluster. This cluster features Dell compute
nodes, each equipped with two 64-core AMD Epyc Milan processors
(128 cores total) and 256 GB of memory. Connectivity is provided by
100 Gbps HDR InfiniBand. The data is stored on a parallel file system
leveraging SFA12k storage platform (Data Direct Networks, USA)
featuring redundant storage arrays across multiple data centers for
maximum availability.
4.1
Indoor imaging data
Table 1 summarizes the data processing of our indoor imaging
dataset. We observed notable differences in input data characteris-
tics and processing times across the different imaging modalities.
We primarily focus on the results from indoor HSI data pro-
cessing because its parallelization across nodes and cores has been
successfully implemented in the workflow. RGB data processing is
not a major part of this discussion due to its minimal computational
overhead. Currently, the X-ray data processing workflow does not
utilize parallelization due to its developmental stage.
The initial HSI processing job script requested 1 core and 30 GB
of memory. However, the SLURM job manager automatically scaled
the resources to 16 CPU cores per task. Limited to 64 cores for con-
current use, we were able to run only four jobs simultaneously to
process all 522 tasks. The total execution time was 216 minutes,
which is less than half the estimated time for asynchronous exe-
cution. We could have achieved a greater speed-up by using more
cores. Another strategy for improving performance could be to
reduce the requested memory, for example, from 30 GB to 15 GB,
which might allow more concurrent jobs to run. However, this
could decrease the number of cores assigned to each job, as our
team’s HPC usage is managed by the system administrator.
4.2
UAV-based imaging data
We evaluated our UAV trait extraction pipeline using data collected
from a field containing 1,280 individual plots (Table 2). The file sizes
of the UAV data varied significantly based on the input imaging
sensor modality. RGB and HSI datasets exhibited the largest file
sizes. This was due to the very fine spatial resolution of the RGB
data and the very high spectral resolution of the HSI data. In
contrast, LiDAR data had a relatively smaller file size, primarily
because of the low pulse density set during flight configuration.
Due to the lack of recurrent thermal data collection at the field sites,
we could not provide a comprehensive analysis of the thermal data.
To assess the performance benefits of parallelization, we con-
ducted all tasks on our HPC system using a fixed configuration.
Although our initial job script requested only a single core and 30
GB of memory, the SLURM job manager automatically scaled the
resources to 16 CPU cores per task. By maintaining this consistent
16-core allocation, we were able to directly measure and compare
time improvements.
We achieved a significant processing speedup by using HPC.
With parallelization, the processing time for our four images was
reduced to approximately 25% for RGB and HSI data. Processing
LiDAR data did not yield a significant speedup. The initial overhead
for DTM generation took 478 seconds. Trait extraction from the
two datasets, which run in parallel in HPC nodes, took 601 seconds
and 190 seconds, respectively, with the time difference attributed
to varying point densities. Parallelization did not yield substantial
performance gains, as the second point cloud processed in 190
seconds, only slightly reducing the total synchronous execution
time from 1269 sec (478+601+190) to 1078 seconds (478+601).
LiDAR data processing remains an area for optimization, specif-
ically concerning spatial indexing. Future work will investigate
techniques like quadtree-based partitioning [13] or tiling, which
involves grouping LiDAR points into regularly-spaced grids and

CONCLUSIONS
Our research successfully applied HPC to HTP in agricultural re-
search, utilizing both indoor and UAV imaging datasets. We demon-
strated a clear and effective solution while detailing bottlenecks in
various imaging sensor modalities, differentiating those occurring
before and during HPC utilization. This paper successfully demon-
strated a novel parallelization strategy for sensor-based plant pheno-
typing, leveraging both HPC node-level and thread-level processing
to significantly boost computational performance. Furthermore, we
compared HPC processing times and resource requirements using
actual indoor and UAV imaging data. While significant progress
has been made, we recognize there is still considerable room for
optimization, particularly in shortening processing time and reduc-
ing memory usage. To achieve further substantial optimization, it
is crucial to migrate license- or operating system-dependent data
processing from individual PCs to HPC systems. This strategic shift
to HPC-based processing using license-free software can address
the primary performance bottlenecks in imaging data workflows,
enabling more efficient and scalable computation.

Abstract: This paper presents a systemic framework designed to advance multi-modal plant phenotyping research through the strategic use of high-performance computing (HPC) in agricultural science. Our framework addresses the unique challenges in high-throughput plant phenotyping (HTP) research, which integrate multi-mode imaging sensors such as RGB, hyperspectral, LiDAR, thermal, and X-ray computed tomography (CT) across indoor and outdoor envi- ronments. Our primary objective is to transform raw sensor data into research-ready plant phenotypical traits. This directly sup- ports downstream agricultural research, such as in plant breeding, crop management, etc. The framework is structured into two main phases. The initial data processing occurs on non-HPC systems, utilizing operating system and license-specific software due to the specialized algorithms and knowledge required for each imaging data pipeline. The subsequent HPC phase refines these processed datasets into tabular formats, preparing them for statistical analysis in agronomy, plant science, and bioinformatics. The current im- plementation of the second phase utilizes a hybrid parallelization model across HPC nodes and threads. However, its performance could be significantly enhanced by implementing more efficient algorithms and optimizing resource allocation. We discuss current bottlenecks, including technical challenges related to sensors, imag- ing platforms, and computational pipelines, and propose immediate solutions.
